description: CosmoSphere is a team passionate about using technology to solve challenges in space exploration and human spaceflight. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we combine software development, science, and creative problem-solving to build innovative, practical solutions. Our focus is on developing technology that supports astronaut health, safety, well-being and mission succes.
summary: Cosmic Shield is an onboard health monitoring and decision-support web app that helps astronauts assess their own physical and mental health on long-duration missions, where help from the ground can be up to 22 minutes away. Crew log vitals, sleep and heart rate variability, glucose, radiation dose, exercise and nutrition, daily mood check-ins, Bristol stool type and vision tests. A transparent, tested rules engine compares each reading with the astronaut’s personal baseline and with thresholds cited from NASA data, showing Normal, Watch or Escalate with clear next steps and when to contact the flight surgeon. Calm early warnings catch patterns such as falling HRV and poor sleep before they grow. Radiation is tracked against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit with DONKI solar event alerts, and each mission environment (ISS, Moon, Mars) adjusts doses, gravity and communication delay. An agentic AI co-pilot explains results using verified data, offers mental health support conversations that escalate concerning messages to the medical team, and supports GI and eye screening through Bristol stool and fundoscope image analysis (prototype). It never diagnoses. Grounded in NASA OSDR, RadLab and DONKI data, Cosmic Shield helps crews act early and stay safe far from Earth.
details:
What it does

Cosmic Shield is an onboard health monitoring and decision-support web app that helps astronauts assess their own physical and mental health during long-duration missions. On the ISS and the moon, help is close, but on Mars a message to the ground can take up to 22 minutes each way, so crews need to notice changes early and know what to do on their own.

How it works: gather, evaluate, act

Crew members log in with an assigned crew ID and PIN, choose their mission environment (ISS, Lunar surface, Mars transit, or Mars surface), and record their health data:

  • Vitals: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, glucose
  • Sleep & Stress: sleep and heart rate variability (HRV)
  • Radiation: dosimeter readings
  • Bone protection: exercise, resistance load, calcium, and vitamin D
  • Mind: daily mood and stress check-ins
  • GI: Bristol stool type and hydration
  • Eyes: Amsler grid vision test and fundoscope images

A deterministic, tested rules engine compares every reading with the astronaut’s own baseline and with cited thresholds and shows Normal, Watch, or Escalate with plain-language guidance and when to contact the Crew Medical Officer or flight surgeon. Pattern rules give calm early warnings, for example, “HRV has dropped for three nights. Sleep is down.” Radiation is tracked against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit, with live or cached solar event alerts from NASA DONKI and projected mission dose for each environment.

An agentic AI co-pilot answers questions by calling tools on the astronaut’s real data (vitals, sleep, radiation, alerts, space weather, NASA baselines) and cites the source of every number. A support conversation on the Mind page offers structured check-ins, and a safety check escalates concerning messages to the medical team. The app never diagnoses or prescribes.

Benefits and impact

Cosmic Shield turns scattered measurements into early, explainable guidance, supporting crew autonomy far from Earth. Streaks and points encourage daily check-ins and exercise, a notification bell reminds crew of due tasks, and a flight-surgeon view lets ground teams review status and escalations while respecting crew privacy.

NASA data

Thresholds and reference values come from:

  • NASA OSDR (Inspiration4 metabolic panel, OSD-575)
  • OSDR RadLab radiation measurements from the ISS, lunar orbit and Mars, including ASI and DLR/ESA instruments
  • DONKI space weather
  • the Human Research Program’s sleep and SANS risks
  • NASA-STD-3001
  • NASA nutrition and exercise sources

Every value is labelled as sourced or app default. Crew data in the demo is simulated and clearly labelled.

Tools and technology

Next.js, React and TypeScript; Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui; Recharts; Zustand; SQLite with Drizzle ORM; Zod; jose and bcryptjs; sharp; Vercel AI SDK; Vitest and Playwright. Open source under the MIT licence.

Creativity and design considerations

  • Mission-specific environments change radiation, gravity, exercise targets, and communication delay.
  • A calm, non-alarming tone throughout.
  • Privacy: chats are never stored, and photos are visible only to the owner and the flight surgeon.
  • Security: hashed PINs, lockout, and session auto-lock.
  • Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast, keyboard navigation, and reduced motion.
  • An offline-first design for spacecraft with limited connectivity.

Use of AI (SI)

We used AI tools during development. Claude Code (Anthropic) assisted with writing, debugging, and testing code, building the NASA data scripts, and drafting documentation. Claude (chat) helped with planning, research, and editing text. Team members reviewed and tested all AI-assisted code and checked every NASA value and threshold against its original source. In the product, the AI co-pilot runs in an offline mock mode by default, with an optional LLM; it explains rule results but never sets a health status. The Bristol and SANS image analysis is a labeled prototype. Full details are in docs/ai-disclosure.md in our repository.
